extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral philosophy; philosophers interested in Kant's ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of Kant's practical-philosophical standards: the claims about what pure practical reason must postulate (immortality, God, freedom), the primacy of practical over speculative reason in certain combinations, and related normative conclusions about morality, the summum bonum, and human dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of practical reason over speculative when combined
rubrics_metrics.description: When pure speculative and pure practical reason are combined in one cognition, the latter has the primacy, provided that this combination is not contingent and arbitrary, but founded a priori on reason itself and therefore necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If practical reason is truly a priori and inseparably connected with certain propositions, speculative reason must accept them as offered from a foreign source and attempt to compare and connect them with its own concepts. This subordination prevents conflict and preserves reason's unity; it is not about mere consistency but about the development and employment of reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summum bonum as the necessary practical object
rubrics_metrics.description: The realization of the summum bonum in the world is the necessary object of a will determinable by the moral law; morality obliges us to make the highest possible good in a world the ultimate object of our conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The summum bonum unites highest moral perfection with happiness proportioned to that morality. Moral law commands the endeavour to promote the summum bonum, but morality itself is not a doctrine of how to become happy — it prescribes worthiness of happiness, not the means of attaining it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immortality of the soul as a postulate
rubrics_metrics.description: Endless progress toward perfect accordance with the moral law (necessary for achieving the summum bonum) presupposes an endless duration of the same rational being — that is, immortality of the soul; thus immortality is a postulate of pure practical reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a practical (not theoretical) postulate: it supplements speculative reason's impotence and gives moral life coherence and hope. The postulate justifies hope (not theoretical certainty) for endless moral progress; it helps avoid degrading the moral law or producing fanatical expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of God as a postulate
rubrics_metrics.description: To render possible the summum bonum (happiness proportioned to morality) in a world, pure practical reason postulates the existence of a cause adequate to harmonize happiness with moral worth — i.e., God; thus the existence of God is morally necessary to assume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This necessity is subjective (a practical want) rather than an objective theoretical duty; the admission functions as a hypothesis or 'pure rational faith' that moral reason uses to make the summum bonum practicably conceivable. It does not ground obligation (which rests on autonomy of reason) but is required for the moral endeavour to realize the summum bonum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom as a necessary supposition (positive consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical reason must postulate freedom positively as the causality of a being insofar as he belongs to the intelligible world; freedom is required for the autonomy that moral law prescribes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freedom is the necessary supposition of independence from the sensible world and the capacity for the will to be determined by intelligible laws. It is a postulate that allows moral responsibility and the concept of an intelligible order in which moral laws govern willing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postulates are practical suppositions, not theoretical dogmas
rubrics_metrics.description: The postulates of immortality, freedom, and God proceed from the principle of morality and are practical necessities (suppositions) rather than theoretical dogmas; they give objective reality to ideas of speculative reason by reference to their practical use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These postulates do not extend speculative knowledge about the nature of souls, the intelligible world, or God; they only render such ideas assertorially real insofar as practical reason requires them for the summum bonum. They justify practical belief without enabling new theoretical (synthetic) knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral law is autonomous and not based on theological knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral law is grounded in the autonomy of reason itself and does not make knowledge of God or His will the foundation of obligation; theology may be postulated for the possibility of the summum bonum, but the authority of moral law remains autonomous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religion or belief in God can be appended to ethics to provide hope of attaining the summum bonum, but this does not change the moral law's status as a priori command of reason; fear or hope must not be the fundamental springs of moral worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morality teaches worthiness of happiness, not techniques for happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Morality is not properly a doctrine of how we should make ourselves happy, but how we should become worthy of happiness; it concerns the rational condition (conditio sine qua non) of happiness, not the means of attaining it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only when religion is added (providing the postulates) does the ethical doctrine become a doctrine of happiness in the sense that hope of happiness becomes possible; nevertheless, moral action must remain motivated by duty, not by pursuit of happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanity as an end in itself
rubrics_metrics.description: In the order of ends, man (and every rational being) is an end in himself and can never be used merely as a means by any, without being also an end in himself; humanity in our person must be treated as holy to ourselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows from being the subject of the moral law founded on autonomy of will. It supplies a normative constraint on actions and institutions: persons must not be treated merely instrumentally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical extension of theoretical reason has limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical reason can make concepts (freedom, immortality, God) assertorially real for practical purposes, extending theoretical reason immanently, but it does not provide speculative cognition of their nature or enable new synthetic theoretical propositions about them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The admission of these postulates allows speculative reason to treat them as having objects for practical ends, but it cannot determine how these conceptions relate to objects or give empirical/intuitive knowledge; thus practical use clears up and constrains speculative misuse (anthropomorphism or fanaticism) without enlarging theoretical knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral ideas as standards (ideas of practical perfection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral ideas (e.g., holiness, the summum bonum) are types of practical perfection that serve as indispensable rules of conduct and standards of comparison; they are not transcendent speculative ideas but guiding ideals for action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calling something an 'idea' of practical perfection does not make it an unknowable transcendent object; rather it functions as a regulative standard that orients moral striving and judgment, e.g., comparing Christian holiness with Greek schools' ideals (simplicity, prudence, wisdom).
